Punta Gorda is a fishing port on the western shore of the Caribbean Sea in southern Belize. The town is a gateway to the many attractions of Toledo District.

River trips depart from here, heading deep into caves and toward Maya archaeological sites.

Situated on Amatique Bay on the Caribbean coast, Punta Gorda suits both relaxed and active holidays. A series of sandy beaches lines the town's waterfront. On Punta Gorda's main street, a market offers a glimpse of local life and the wider culture of Belize, with handmade crafts from across the country.

The town also provides convenient access to the important Maya archaeological sites of Nim Li Punit and Lubaantun, as well as the Port Honduras Marine Reserve, home to manatees and other rare animals.

### Punta Cana — a taste of paradise!

Punta Cana looks like a destination straight out of a tropical paradise advertisement. The resort lies on the eastern coast of the Dominican Republic and is home to one of the country's three international airports. Much of this small town's long coastline is lined with low-rise five-star hotels catering to families and travelers seeking peaceful holidays surrounded by nature. Nearby, visitors can explore three national parks and mangrove forests and see reptiles and tropical birds.

Beaches are Punta Cana's main attraction. For a more secluded day by the sea, head to Macao, one of the most environmentally pristine spots on the eastern coast.

## Beach holidays in Punta Cana

### Punta Cana — spectacular beaches in the Dominican Republic!

Cap Cana is an exclusive area with white-sand beaches, luxury hotels, green palms and swimming pools. Bávaro is Punta Cana's liveliest beach, with bars and nightclubs. Divers can explore the warm Caribbean Sea, with colorful corals, tropical fish, underwater grottoes and shipwrecks. Punta Cana and its surroundings also offer plenty of attractions to complement a leisurely beach holiday with excursions to parks, lagoons, islands, waterfalls and coral reefs.

At Punta Moreno, the first thing you see is dark lava stretching toward the foot of Cerro Azul on Isabela Island. Folds and uneven ridges cover the surface, with the first plants taking root among them. Then, small lagoons appear amid the rocky landscape. The water reflects the sky, and your eyes begin searching for movement along its edge.

Flamingos, ducks and other waterbirds frequent these small pools. Their pink plumage stands out against the black rock. As you follow the trail, it is worth looking at each lagoon individually: some are open and still, while others are surrounded by plants. The contrast between solidified lava and living water makes the walk rich in detail.

Punta Moreno appeals to travelers who enjoy walking across volcanic terrain and watching birds. The uneven lava encourages an unhurried pace, so comfortable footwear helps you focus on the scenery. Bring binoculars and take your time: the most interesting sights here often appear in a small mirror of water among the rocks.

At Punta Suárez on Española Island, keep an eye on both the ground and your surroundings: the rocky trail passes through wildlife habitat. Sea lions rest along the shore, and marine iguanas bask on the lava. Farther on, colonies of boobies catch your attention, while the silhouettes of other seabirds flash across the ocean sky.

During the nesting season, usually from April to December, Galápagos albatrosses can be seen here. Their large bodies, long yellow bills and measured movements make it worth lingering beside the trail. Nature lovers can watch the birds going about their daily lives and then follow their flight over the water.

The walk leads to coastal cliffs. Waves surge into a fissure in the lava and shoot a fountain of spray upward; its height depends on sea conditions. Salty air, dark stone and white foam complete the experience of this headland. Punta Suárez rewards travelers who have time to observe an individual bird or iguana and discover Española through such encounters.

Purmamarca's streets have retained the traditional appearance of northern Argentina: low houses built of clay and stone, small craft shops, welcoming squares and colorful local markets. It is a wonderful place for an unhurried stroll, browsing the work of local artisans and soaking up the atmosphere of a region where European traditions mingle with the cultural heritage of the Andes.

The main natural attraction is Cerro de los Siete Colores, or the Hill of Seven Colors. Its multicolored layers formed over millions of years as a result of differences in the composition of the rock. Shades of red, pink, ochre, green and gray are especially striking in the morning and evening light.

Purmamarca is also a starting point for exploring the surrounding mountain scenery. One of the most impressive walks follows the Paseo de los Colorados, offering panoramic views of colorful cliffs and the valley.

Purmamarca reveals a different side of Argentina: ancient Andean culture, unusual geology, characterful settlements and landscapes unlike those found anywhere else in the country.
